clue.text: Description of Willy Wonka in a 1967 novel partly about a factory

definitions.meaning: Roald Dahl's chocolate maker is a man who sells confectionery

definitions.text: a 1967 novel partly about a factory
definitions.meaning: R. K. Narayan's 1967 novel about the confectioner Jagan, whose son plans a factory for story-writing machines

explanation.walkthrough: 'in' only joins the two definitions. Narayan's title carries a leading 'The' that the grid drops.
explanation.definitionFit: A fair label for Dahl's confectioner, and (less its opening article) the title of R. K. Narayan's Malgudi book about Jagan.

clue.text: Novel list includes an American source of satire

indicators.note: includes says the two words before it hold the name within their run of letters

explanation.surface: A fresh reading list features a US work full of mockery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'includes' points back at 'Novel list', where the surname spans the two words. Bret Easton Ellis wrote American Psycho, a satire of 1980s Wall Street.
explanation.definitionFit: Bret Easton, the US novelist of American Psycho and Less Than Zero, writes satirical fiction.

clue.text: Treatment of Word and cloths roles in a Victorian seminary

indicators.note: treatment means working over, so the three words that follow are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A study of how scripture, vestments and duties were handled at a nineteenth-century college for priests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Treatment of' rearranges WORD, CLOTHS and ROLES; 'and' only joins them. Seminary is an old word for a school, and this is Trollope's 1881 novel about a clergyman's boys' academy.
explanation.definitionFit: Trollope's 1881 novel is named after a clergyman's private academy for boys, and seminary once meant any such place of education.

clue.text: King united with queen in a famous Czech play

parts.note: R is short for rex, Latin for king
U is the abbreviation for united, as in football club names
R is short for regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: A monarch is joined with his consort in a celebrated drama from Prague.
explanation.walkthrough: Karel Capek's 1920 drama, short for Rossum's Universal Robots, gave the world the word robot. 'with' and 'in' only link.
explanation.definitionFit: Karel Capek's 1920 drama, Rossum's Universal Robots, is known by these initials.

clue.text: "May I a small house, and large garden have! / And a few and many books, both true" (Abraham Cowley)

definitions.text: "May I a small house, and large garden have! / And a few and many books, both true" (Abraham Cowley)

parts.words: "May I a small house, and large garden have! / And a few and many books, both true" (Abraham Cowley)
parts.note: a quotation with one word left out after 'a few': the missing word from Cowley's poem The Wish is what is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: No wordplay: the quotation has a word missing after 'a few'. Cowley's poem The Wish asks for a few companions and many books, 'both true'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the missing word of Cowley's line: a few true companions set beside many true books.

clue.text: A miner with everything, including sought-after rock after some time

indicators.note: including says the word for the whole lot holds the other two pieces inside it

parts.note: all means everything

indicators.note: after sends the mined rock second, behind the word for a period of time, although the clue names it first

parts.note: a term is a fixed period of time, as at school or in office
ore is rock that is mined for the metal it holds

explanation.surface: A pitman who has all he wants, valuable stone included, after a while.
explanation.walkthrough: He is the coal-miner father in D. H. Lawrence's Sons and Lovers. 'including' and 'after' fix the order: the period first, then the rock, both inside the word for everything.
explanation.definitionFit: He is Paul's father in D. H. Lawrence's Sons and Lovers, a Nottinghamshire collier.

clue.text: This deceased person wrote novels about war — did Fred Green?

indicators.note: about means moving around, so the letters of the three short words beside it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
a green is a grassy field, as in village green

explanation.surface: A dead author produced fiction on warfare, and someone asks whether a man called Fred Green did too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges WAR DID FRED into EDWARDDRIF. He is the celebrated novelist, recently dead when the story opens, in Somerset Maugham's Cakes and Ale.
explanation.definitionFit: In Somerset Maugham's Cakes and Ale he is the grand old man of letters whose life is being written after his death.

clue.text: An unpleasant character in Jane Eyre is Charlie, covered in excrement by cattle

definitions.text: An unpleasant character in Jane Eyre

parts.note: scat is the term for animal droppings
Charlie is the word for C in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a herd is a group of cattle

explanation.surface: A nasty figure in the Bronte novel is a fool who ends up smeared with dung next to the cows.
explanation.walkthrough: She is the teacher at Lowood who persecutes Helen Burns. In a down entry 'covered in' means the droppings lie on top of Charlie's letter, and 'by' sets the cattle alongside.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the Lowood teacher who bullies and flogs Helen Burns.

clue.text: Iris could be this kind of female vendor

parts.note: an iris is a garden plant grown for its bloom
Iris is also a woman's first name, so an example of a young female

explanation.surface: A woman called Iris might be the sort who sells things for a living.
explanation.walkthrough: One word does two turns: Iris the bloom gives the first word, Iris the woman's name the second. 'could be' marks both as examples.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone like Eliza Doolittle, a young woman selling blooms in the street, is a seller of this sort.

clue.text: This could make you blue some money, gaining nothing

indicators.note: gaining says the bundle of cash takes an extra letter into itself

parts.note: a wad is a roll or bundle of banknotes
nothing is zero, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: Something that depresses you: a bit of cash that earns no return.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blue' reads as sad, but it is the colour: ancient Britons dyed their skin with this plant. 'gaining' puts O into WAD.
explanation.definitionFit: The plant yields the indigo dye that ancient Britons painted on their bodies, literally turning them that colour.

clue.text: Victim of anonymous attacks, stage right, on bum

indicators.note: bum as an adjective means dud or faulty, so the letters before it are out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man targeted by unsigned abuse stands at the side of the theatre, sitting on his backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bum' rearranges STAGE, R and ON. In Beckett's Waiting for Godot this tramp says he is beaten every night by people he cannot name, hence the anonymous attacks; the theatre wording is apt for a stage character.
explanation.definitionFit: Beckett's tramp in Waiting for Godot reports being beaten nightly by unnamed assailants.

clue.text: Strong door I destroyed in a spell of violence

indicators.note: destroyed means broken up, so the letters of the three words before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: In a fit of rage I smashed a sturdy door to pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'destroyed' rearranges STRONG DOOR I. These were the anti-Catholic disturbances in London in 1780, the setting of Dickens's Barnaby Rudge.
explanation.definitionFit: They were days of anti-Catholic mob disorder in London in 1780, as in Barnaby Rudge.

clue.text: One of three kings in Shakespearean plays in Italy

definitions.text: One of three kings in Shakespearean plays in Italy

parts.words: One of three kings in Shakespearean plays in Italy
parts.note: Shakespeare wrote history plays about Henry IV, Henry V and Henry VI; in Italy the name Henry takes its Italian form

explanation.walkthrough: 'in Italy' does not place the plays there: it asks for the Italian form of the name shared by three of Shakespeare's title kings, Henry IV, V and VI.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian equivalent of Henry, the name of three consecutive monarchs with history plays to their name.

clue.text: Snout's barrier (or septum)

definitions.meaning: in A Midsummer Night's Dream Tom Snout the tinker plays the partition between Pyramus and Thisbe
a septum is a dividing partition in the body, such as the one between the nostrils

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all about a nose, but Snout is Tom Snout the tinker in A Midsummer Night's Dream, who plays the partition dividing the lovers.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are partitions: the part Tom Snout acts in the mechanicals' play, and anatomically a dividing membrane.

clue.text: Saving dimes for a disaster

indicators.note: a disaster is a wreck, so the three words before it are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Putting small coins by in case catastrophe strikes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saving' looks like thrift but is the preposition meaning except. 'disaster' rearranges DIMES FOR A.
explanation.definitionFit: Saving is an old-fashioned preposition meaning except or apart from.

clue.text: Kind of pink flower going further up the wall

parts.note: a rose is a familiar garden bloom
to go up the wall is to become mad, so going further up it is becoming more mad

explanation.surface: A pink climbing plant that keeps creeping higher up the brickwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind of pink flower' seems one phrase; the definition stops at 'pink'. 'up the wall' is British slang for crazy, so further up it is crazier.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an artist's pigment of a pinkish-red shade, made from the root of a dye plant.

clue.text: A female petty criminal in Dickens fiction changing character initially becomes an old literary lady

parts.note: Miss is the title of an unmarried woman

indicators.note: the first letter (character) of the pickpocket's name is swapped for another, here D for C

parts.note: the Artful Dodger is the young pickpocket in Oliver Twist

explanation.surface: A woman thief out of Dickens is rewritten and turns into an elderly bookish dame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing character initially' swaps the first D of DODGER for C; the clue does not say which letter comes in. In Martin Chuzzlewit she is one of two 'literary ladies' Martin meets in America, and her surname itself means an old person.
explanation.definitionFit: In Martin Chuzzlewit she is introduced as one of two bluestockings, and her surname is slang for an elderly person.

clue.text: Italian craftsman's approach includes training

indicators.note: includes says the phrase for approach holds the abbreviation inside it

parts.note: to approach a place is to get to it
PE is physical education, exercise taught at school

explanation.surface: The way an artisan from Italy works involves an apprenticeship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'includes' puts PE inside GET TO. He is the woodcarver who makes Pinocchio, here in the one-P spelling some English versions use.
explanation.definitionFit: He is the woodcarver who makes the puppet Pinocchio in Collodi's story.

clue.text: Kind of sporting contest that's popular with dirty sides

parts.note: something popular is in, meaning in fashion

indicators.note: the sides of a word are its first and last letters, here those of dirty

explanation.surface: A sort of match the crowds love when both teams play foul.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sides' reads as teams but takes the first and last letters of 'dirty'. The answer is short for IndyCar, the American open-wheel motor racing of the Indianapolis 500.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the short name for American open-wheel motor racing, as in the Indianapolis 500.

clue.text: In fiction, Christine from Plymouth or a coastal town in Yorkshire

definitions.meaning: Stephen King's novel Christine is about a possessed 1958 Plymouth Fury, a scarlet automobile
a seaside resort near Middlesbrough on the North Yorkshire coast

explanation.walkthrough: Christine sounds like a Devon woman; she is the haunted Plymouth Fury of Stephen King's novel, a scarlet automobile. Read as two words that description is the resort's name.
explanation.definitionFit: King's Plymouth Fury is a scarlet motor vehicle, and run together those two words name a seaside resort near Middlesbrough.

clue.text: Role for Buster Keaton or Bob Hope's friend, carefree at heart and very competent

definitions.text: Role for Buster Keaton or Bob Hope

parts.note: a pal is a friend

indicators.note: at heart points to the central letters of the word carefree

parts.note: an ace is someone extremely skilled, and as an adjective means first-rate

explanation.surface: A part for either comedian's chum, who is easygoing deep down and thoroughly capable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at heart' takes EF from the centre of 'carefree'. Keaton made The Paleface in 1922 and Hope a western comedy of the same name in 1948. The possessive after Hope links to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Both comedians starred in a film of this title, Keaton in 1922 and Hope in the 1948 western spoof.

clue.text: Salisbury's name before 1868

parts.note: the Victorian prime minister became Marquess of Salisbury in 1868; before inheriting the title he went by his family surname, as Lord Robert

explanation.walkthrough: Not the cathedral city: the Victorian prime minister inherited the title Marquess of Salisbury in 1868, and before that was known by the family surname.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the family surname of the Victorian prime minister, who was Lord Robert before inheriting his marquessate.

clue.text: A short description of Thelma and Louise, rejected as a Bond film

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the letters of the abbreviated phrase run backwards

parts.words: A short description of Thelma and Louise
parts.note: Thelma & Louise is a road movie, so its heroines are on the road, shortened to ON RD

explanation.surface: A brief pitch for a film about two women was turned down as a spy picture.
explanation.walkthrough: The two women spend their film on the road; 'short' abbreviates road to RD, and 'rejected' turns ON RD back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the first James Bond picture, released in 1962.

clue.text: Post-nuclear story with strand on someone absorbing thorium

indicators.note: on here means added to, the shore word following the piece it is attached to
absorbing says the word for a person takes the chemical symbol inside it

parts.note: one is a pronoun for an unspecified person
Th is the chemical symbol for thorium
a strand is a shore or stretch of sand by the sea

explanation.surface: A tale set after the bomb, with one thread about a person taking in radioactive metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strand' looks like a plot thread but is a seashore; 'absorbing' and 'on' do the assembling. The novel is Nevil Shute's, about Australians waiting for fallout to reach them.
explanation.definitionFit: Nevil Shute's 1957 novel follows Australians awaiting fallout after an atomic war.

clue.text: Finally make book concise, or earlier, make it longer

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letters of the three words that follow it

explanation.surface: In the end cut the volume down, or before that pad it out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' takes the last letters of 'make book concise'. 'earlier' marks the old sense of the word, to lengthen or add to; 'or' links.
explanation.definitionFit: In older English the verb meant to increase or lengthen, a sense surviving in 'eke out'.

clue.text: Historic translator's note: The French read "clove" differently

parts.note: mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale
les is a French word for the, in the plural

indicators.note: differently says the letters of the two words before it are put in another order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A footnote from an old translator records that the French understood the word clove another way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'translator's note' is not one phrase: the possessive ends the definition and 'note' is a musical one. 'differently' turns the last two words into the surname of the man behind the 1535 English Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: He produced the first complete printed English Bible, in 1535.
